system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
Metabolic/toxic injury of central white matter
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: During chronic hyponatremia, brain cells adapt by losing inorganic ions and organic osmolytes to limit cerebral edema. If extracellular tonicity then rises too quickly during correction, osmolyte-depleted cells cannot restore intracellular solute rapidly enough; water leaves the cells, producing osmotic cellular injury, blood-brain-barrier/glial dysfunction, and noninflammatory demyelination, classically in the central pons.
vignette: A 54-year-old man with alcohol use disorder and poor nutritional intake is hospitalized with chronic severe hyponatremia. His serum sodium concentration is corrected rapidly. He initially becomes more alert, but several days later develops dysarthria, dysphagia, and symmetric weakness of all four extremities. MRI shows a symmetric T2-hyperintense lesion in the central pons without a vascular-territory pattern.
lead: Which pathophysiologic process most directly explains this neurologic deterioration?
correct: Rapid extracellular hypertonicity causes water loss from brain cells that had adapted to chronic hyponatremia by depleting intracellular osmolytes, leading to demyelination
distractors: Persistent cerebral edema caused by continued intracellular accumulation of osmolytes during chronic hyponatremia
Autoantibody-mediated destruction of central myelin following a recent viral infection
Thiamine deficiency causing hemorrhagic injury of the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray matter
Occlusion of perforating branches of the basilar artery causing an ischemic pontine infarction
distractor_notes: Chronic hyponatremia triggers loss—not continued accumulation—of intracellular osmolytes as an adaptation against swelling. The danger arises when extracellular tonicity is then raised faster than brain cells can reacquire osmolytes.

Postinfectious immune-mediated demyelination can occur in acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, but the temporal relationship to correction of chronic hyponatremia and the classic central pontine pattern indicate osmotic rather than autoimmune injury.

Alcohol use and malnutrition raise concern for Wernicke encephalopathy, but thiamine deficiency preferentially affects mammillary bodies, medial thalami and periaqueductal regions and does not explain delayed central pontine demyelination after sodium correction.

Basilar perforator ischemia can cause pontine deficits, but the symmetric central lesion appearing days after rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia is the classic nonvascular pattern of osmotic demyelination.
key_expl: The patient has osmotic demyelination syndrome. In chronic hyponatremia, brain cells defend against swelling by extruding electrolytes and then organic osmolytes. This adaptation lowers intracellular osmotic content. If serum tonicity rises abruptly during treatment, extracellular fluid becomes relatively hypertonic before brain cells can replenish their osmolytes; water moves out of cells and causes osmotic injury to glial/myelin units. The central pons is especially susceptible, although extrapontine sites may also be affected. Modern evidence implicates early astrocyte injury as part of the cascade, so the mechanism should not be reduced to isolated oligodendrocyte shrinkage.
objective: Explain osmotic demyelination after correction of chronic hyponatremia as injury to an osmolyte-depleted brain exposed to a rapid rise in extracellular tonicity.
clues: rapid rise in serum sodium during treatment
initial clinical improvement followed by delayed neurologic decline

sources.support: NCBI explains that chronic hyponatremia causes loss of intracellular ions and organic osmolytes; rapid correction prevents timely osmolyte recovery, causes brain-cell dehydration and demyelination, often centered in the pons, with neurologic deterioration emerging after correction.
